newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-New Brazil forex band means no policy change.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-New Brazil forex band means no policy change.

text.p: When the Brazilian central bank set a new large trading band for its currency on Tuesday, it was confirming that it had no plans to speed up depreciation of the real, reasserting its committment to the current forex policy, economists said.
The central bank lowered the large band to between 1.05 and 1.14 reais to the dollar from a previous range of 0.97 to 1.06 reais set on January 30, 1996.

Economists said the change would allow for about a 7.4 percent depreciation of the currency in 1997 and signaled the central bank was not prepared to accelerate depreciation to reverse a burgeoning trade deficit.

"From tomorrow everything will be absolutely as it has been," said Gustavo Franco, the central bank's international affairs director. "We are continuing with something we started one and a half years ago," he said, referring to the introduction of the interband foreign exchange rate policy in March 1995.

Since then, the currency has traded on a daily basis within a mini-band, which is depreciated slightly about six times a month. As the mini-band ceiling approaches the ceiling of the large band, the central bank sets a new large band.
To reassure the markets and avoid speculation when trading begins on Wednesday, the bank set a new mini-band of between 1.050 and 1.055 reais per dollar, effective Wednesday.

Before Tuesday's move, the Brazilian press speculated that the central bank was considering doing away with the double band system and relying solely on a wider mini-band to free up trade and reduce speculation in the futures market.

To be sure, the media and market participants have also speculated about the possibility of a speedier depreciation of the Brazilian currency to slow a mounting trade gap that reached $5.5 billion last year.
But economists said the decision to maintain the existing policy was widely expected.

"This is well within market expectations. This doesn't change our estimate for a 7.2 percent depreciation of the reais against the dollar in 1997," said Dany Rappaport, chief economist at MCM Consultores in Brazil.
Currency traders also welcomed the move. "The market is going to react favorably to the new band and the mini-band," said one trader.

For the past several months, the futures market has seen bouts of speculation on a faster depreciation of the reais, as traders bet the government would have to resort to tinkering with the exchange rate to slow the growth in imports.
But the central bank has repeatedly stated that under no circumstances would it use foreign exchange policy as a tool to boost exports.
